lines: Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon argues Jensen Huang's dismissal leaves Nvidia with acute key-man risk: near-term operations look stable, but the long-term strategic vision and personal handshake deals with supply-chain partners were his.

The episode says the decisive trigger for the board was undisclosed relationships with subordinates and dishonesty toward the board, rather than the espionage and geopolitical concerns that dominated early coverage.
Rasgon flags Nvidia's highly centralized decision-making with no formal succession plan, plus brain-drain risk as many already-wealthy employees may not stay through the transition.
The 'Bank of AI' strategy of committing capital to secure supply-chain capacity, driven by Huang's personal conviction, and the durability of the CUDA moat may both be re-tested under new leadership.

On policy, the show argues that restricting even older-generation chip sales to China could speed its self-sufficient AI ecosystem, and that public infighting in Washington makes chip export rules increasingly unpredictable.
title: How Wall Street Is Bracing For the Post-Jensen Huang Nvidia Era
